message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This bid is unusual in that it is not based on assumptions about demand: we tested the exact opening pattern at Ashgrove before asking for a penny, and measured the results hour by hour. The pilot showed strong uptake, with evening visits running close to daytime levels and Sunday sessions very popular with families, and new memberships up by about two-thirds on the year before. That gives Members real local evidence that the hours will be used. The costing is equally careful. Staffing is built up from first principles, hours times staff times weeks times branches at the correct graded rate with on-costs, and utilities are taken from actual pilot spend rather than estimates, all of which sums to £174,000. We also looked seriously at the cheaper self-service alternative and explain why it would cost more once building works are included. I am confident this is a well-tested, carefully costed proposal that delivers on the Council Plan.
</author>

<document>
Budget Justification: Extended Opening Hours at Five Branch Libraries, 2027-28
Library Services, Westmoor Borough Council, September 2026

1. Request
Library Services requests a growth bid of £174,000 in the 2027-28 revenue budget to extend opening hours at five branch libraries (Ashgrove, Fenwick, Holt Lane, Kingsmead and Millbrook) by ten hours a week each, from 38 to 48 hours.

2. Rationale
The five branches currently close at 5 pm on weekdays and do not open on Sundays. Residents' surveys have repeatedly identified opening hours as the main barrier to library use among working-age adults: in the 2025 Residents' Survey, 44% of non-users aged 25-54 said the library "is never open when I can go". The Council Plan commits to increasing library use among working-age residents and to supporting adult learning and job-seeking.

Each branch would add late opening until 8 pm on Tuesdays and Thursdays (six additional hours) and Sunday opening from 11 am to 3 pm (four additional hours).

3. Evidence from the Ashgrove pilot
From October 2025 to March 2026, Ashgrove trialled exactly this pattern, funded from one-off underspends.

Table 1. Ashgrove pilot: average visits per opening hour, October 2025 to March 2026
Time slot | Visits per hour
Weekday 9 am - 12 pm | 46
Weekday 12 pm - 5 pm | 58
Tuesday and Thursday 5 pm - 8 pm (new) | 21
Saturday 9 am - 1 pm | 64
Sunday 11 am - 3 pm (new) | 52

Over the pilot, Ashgrove recorded 1,140 new library memberships, compared with 690 in the same months a year earlier. Sunday sessions were particularly popular with families, and a weekly job club in the Thursday evening slot was fully booked from its third week.

Evening visits at Ashgrove averaged close to the weekday daytime level, which shows that there is strong latent demand for evening opening and that the new hours will be well used across all five branches.

4. Costs
Additional hours need two staff on duty at all times, in line with the Council's lone-working policy. Staffing is calculated on 50 weeks a year, allowing for bank holiday closures.

Table 2. Cost of extended hours, five branches
Item | Basis | Cost
Staffing | 10 hours x 2 staff x 50 weeks x 5 branches = 5,000 hours at £24.80 per hour (including on-costs) | £124,000
Utilities and caretaking | £6,500 per branch | £32,500
Self-service kiosk upgrades (maintenance contract) | 5 branches | £7,500
Total | | £174,000

The staffing rate is the mid-point of the Library Assistant grade plus 28% on-costs and an enhancement for Sunday working. Utilities and caretaking costs are based on the actual additional costs recorded at Ashgrove during the pilot, scaled to a full year.

5. Value for money
At current visit rates, the extra hours across the five branches would generate roughly 84,000 additional visits a year, at a cost of around £2 per visit. This compares favourably with the borough's average cost per library visit of £3.40.

6. Alternatives considered
We considered opening the branches with self-service access only in the extra hours, as some authorities have done. This would cut staffing costs by around two-thirds, but the Council's insurers have advised that unstaffed opening would require building alterations and CCTV at an estimated £60,000 per branch, and it would not support the job club and family activities that drove much of the pilot's success.

7. Risks
Recruitment. We expect to fill most additional hours from existing part-time staff who have asked for more hours, as happened during the pilot.
Demand at other branches. Ashgrove is our busiest branch, and demand at the other four may be lower. We will review usage after six months.

8. Conclusion
The twelve-month Ashgrove pilot has demonstrated strong demand for evening and Sunday opening, with new memberships up by two-thirds and evening use close to daytime levels. We ask Members to approve a growth bid of £174,000 to extend this successful model to all five branches from April 2027.
</document>
response:
# Review: Extended Opening Hours Budget Justification

**The bid has a genuine strength: a real pilot with measured results. But several of the author's specific claims don't hold up against the document itself.**

- The table doesn't add up to £174,000.
- Evening use was well under half of daytime levels, not "close to" them.
- The pilot ran for six months, not twelve.
- The paper never shows that the self-service option "would cost more."

The Sunday results are strong and the case for extended hours may well stand, but the paper needs correcting before it goes to Members.

## 1. The total is wrong

Table 2: £124,000 + £32,500 + £7,500 = **£164,000, not £174,000**.

Each line is correct on its own terms; for example, 10 × 2 × 50 × 5 = 5,000 hours at £24.80 = £124,000. Either there is a £10,000 arithmetic error, or a cost line has been left out of the table. Members will be asked to approve £174,000, so this has to be resolved.

## 2. Evening demand is overstated

The paper says evening visits "averaged close to the weekday daytime level." The author's summary says they ran "close to daytime levels." Table 1 shows otherwise:

| Slot | Visits/hour | Evening as % of slot |
|---|---|---|
| Weekday 9–12 | 46 | 46% |
| Weekday 12–5 | 58 | 36% |
| **Tue/Thu 5–8 (new)** | **21** | — |

Evening use was **about 36–46% of daytime**. That is still worthwhile demand: the fully booked job club is a good sign. But it doesn't show the "strong latent demand" the paper claims.

**Sunday is the real success.** At 52 visits an hour, it is close to weekday afternoons and not far below Saturday. The paper would be more convincing if it led with Sunday and presented evenings honestly.

## 3. The pilot was six months, not twelve

Section 3 says the pilot ran from October 2025 to March 2026. The Conclusion calls it "the twelve-month Ashgrove pilot." The correct length is six months, covering autumn and winter only.

That matters in two ways:
- **Seasonality.** Evening use in light summer months may differ from winter.
- **Scaling the utilities.** The £6,500 per branch utility figure comes from winter spend scaled to a full year. That probably *overstates* the annual cost, because heating and lighting peak in winter, so this error happens to be cautious. Note also that the figure comes from one branch and is applied to all five.

## 4. The self-service comparison doesn't show what the author claims

The author says the paper explains why self-service "would cost more once building works are included." The paper doesn't do that.

- **Annual saving:** cutting staffing by about two-thirds would save about **£83,000 a year**.
- **One-off works:** building alterations and CCTV would cost £60,000 × 5 = **£300,000**, once.
- **Break-even:** after about **3.6 years**, self-service would be cheaper. It's also capital rather than revenue spending, which may matter for budgeting.

So self-service costs more in year one but less over the longer term. The stronger argument against it is the one the paper already makes in passing: unstaffed hours can't support the job club or family activities. The paper should rest its case on that, not on cost.

## 5. Value for money is optimistic

- **Visit numbers.** The 84,000 figure is calculated correctly from Ashgrove's rates: (21 × 6 + 52 × 4) × 50 weeks × 5 branches ≈ 83,500. But the Risks section says Ashgrove is the busiest branch and the others "may be lower." The figure assumes all five match it.
  - For illustration, if the other four branches managed 60% of Ashgrove's rate, there would be about 57,000 visits.
  - That puts the cost per visit at about £2.90 on £164,000, or about £3.05 on £174,000.
- **"Additional" visits.** Some evening and Sunday visitors would otherwise have come during existing hours. Not every visit in the new hours is an extra one.
- **The £3.40 comparison isn't like-for-like.** The borough average cost per visit almost certainly includes buildings, stock and management. The £2 figure is a marginal cost. The comparison flatters the bid.

## 6. Other points to check

- **Current hours.** Table 1 shows weekdays 9 am–5 pm plus Saturday 9 am–1 pm. That is 44 hours, but Section 1 says branches currently open 38. Either there are lunch closures or a closed weekday, or one of the figures is wrong.
- **Membership growth.** 1,140 against 690 is indeed up about two-thirds (+65%). But this is a before-and-after comparison at one branch with no control, so other factors such as publicity or novelty can't be ruled out. It also covers all membership growth, not just sign-ups during the new hours.
- **Blended staffing rate.** £24.80 includes a Sunday enhancement but is applied to all 5,000 hours, including evenings. That makes it a blended estimate, not "the correct graded rate" as the author describes it. The paper should show how the blend is weighted.
- **Self-service kiosk upgrades (£7,500).** It isn't explained why a staffed option needs kiosk upgrades.
- **50 weeks.** This is a reasonable allowance, although most bank holidays fall on Mondays, which aren't extended hours anyway.

## 7. What's sound

- Running a real pilot of the exact pattern before bidding is good practice.
- The Residents' Survey evidence (44% of non-users aged 25–54) and the link to the Council Plan are clear and relevant.
- The staffing calculation and the two-staff lone-working requirement are well explained.
- The risk section is candid about Ashgrove being unrepresentative and about recruitment.
- The non-financial case against self-service (job club, families) is a legitimate reason to prefer staffed opening.

## Recommended changes

1. Fix the total, or add the missing £10,000 line and explain it.
2. Describe evening use accurately, at about 40% of daytime, and lead with the Sunday results.
3. Correct "twelve-month" to six months and acknowledge that the pilot covered winter only.
4. Reframe the self-service section around service quality. If cost is mentioned, show the 3–4 year break-even honestly.
5. Give a visit range for the other four branches rather than assuming they match Ashgrove, and drop or qualify the £3.40 comparison.
6. Reconcile the 38 current hours with the 44 implied by Table 1.

If you'd like, I can draft revised versions of Sections 3, 5 and 6 and the Conclusion.
